name: phase02-batch

version.prompts: P1 2026-11-08 (owner: Phase 02 reference batches 2a + 2b live acceptance, 13 prompts)
version.labels: L1 2026-11-08 kinds, expected references and Core/Optional sketches written from the batch-2a (c629726824) and batch-2b (7988753b25) handoffs before any card

measures: Live /explain acceptance of the batch 2a and 2b references: which references each card received, the chosen kind (two-panel composition or not), the card's own arithmetic, formula rendering, narrow-card fit and save/reload. Run once at --depth standard.
written: 2026-11-08, before any phase02-batch card was sent
notation: As the content set: best/acceptable mixes (P = picture, D:<kind> = a TutorDiagram, D:a|b = either kind, D:* = any kind); kinds = the right kinds; sketch lines "Core:" = what the diagram must show, "Optional:" = extras. references = the reference ids the selector is expected to send (from the handoff tables; the dev log line explanation_author_raw records the actual ids). The reference numbers are illustrative: a card is checked on its own data.

prompts.prompt: How can ordered categories be represented by numbers?
sketch: Core: A declared meaningful order of the categories (e.g. Low < Medium < High), its numeric codebook (0, 1, 2), and observations encoded consistently with that one codebook; the codes rank the categories but do not prove equal gaps between them.
Optional: A contrast with one-hot encoding for unordered categories.

prompts.prompt: Which bucket does a number on a bin edge belong to?
sketch: Core: The interval convention stated (e.g. [a, b) with a closed final bin), and every raw value assigned to an explicit bin, including a value exactly on an internal edge and one on the final boundary.
Optional: Bin counts that agree with the memberships (a histogram or a count column).

prompts.prompt: Why add a feature that multiplies two inputs?
sketch: Core: Both original inputs (x1, x2) stay visible per row, the product x1 x2 is computed per row, and the card says why one feature changes the effect of the other.
Optional: The model term w x1 x2 or a plot of the effect at two values of the other input.

prompts.prompt: What happens to a skewed distribution when we take logs?
sketch: Core: The same observations on the raw scale and after the stated log transform (e.g. log(1+x)), as matched histograms whose bins are explicit; the long right tail is compressed; the valid domain of the transform is stated.
Optional: The paired raw and transformed value of each observation.

prompts.prompt: Why do precision and recall divide by different totals?
sketch: Core: One set of confusion-matrix counts; precision = TP / (TP + FP) over the predicted positives and recall = TP / (TP + FN) over the actual positives, each denominator's population named, with the two rates computed from those counts.
Optional: Specificity TN / (TN + FP) over the actual negatives.

prompts.prompt: Why is RMSE bigger than MAE when one prediction is far off?
sketch: Core: One shared residual set with each absolute and squared error; MAE = mean |e| and RMSE = sqrt(mean e^2) computed from it; the one large residual dominates the squares, so RMSE > MAE.
Optional: MSE stated before the square root; the residuals drawn as segments on a plot.

prompts.prompt: Show two histograms comparing raw and log-transformed values.
sketch: Core: Two histograms of the same observations, one raw and one log-transformed, each with explicit bins; the raw one is right-skewed and the log one is more even; the transform is stated.
Optional: The transform's valid domain and the paired values.
prompts.note: Required-kind path: a comparison counts as right only when its panels are histograms; a single histogram diagram counts only if it shows both distributions (checked by hand).

prompts.prompt: Why does fitting the same model on different samples give different predictions?
sketch: Core: Lines fitted to different training samples drawn on matching axes; their predictions at one x differ; the mean and the observed range of those predictions.
Optional: The training points of each fit; the link to variance.

prompts.prompt: How can soft voting pick a different class from the majority vote?
sketch: Core: Each model's normalized class probabilities; the hard vote counts each model's top class and the soft vote averages the probabilities, and the two pick different classes.
Optional: The averaged probability of each class stated as a percentage.

prompts.prompt: What happens to the training weights after AdaBoost gets one example wrong?
sketch: Core: The same rows before and after; the weighted error of the miss, the coefficient alpha = (1/2) ln((1 - err) / err), the missed row's weight raised and the correct rows' lowered, renormalized to sum 1.
Optional: The next weak learner focusing on the missed row.

prompts.prompt: Where do the out-of-fold predictions for the stacking model come from?
sketch: Core: Which rows train each base model in each fold and which held-out rows it predicts; each held-out row's base-model predictions joined with its target into one meta-training row.
Optional: The meta-model trained on those rows.

prompts.prompt: How does Bayesian optimization decide which setting to try next?
sketch: Core: Candidate settings with the surrogate's mean and uncertainty, an acquisition score per candidate computed from them (e.g. UCB = mean + k x sd), and the highest-scoring candidate chosen even when another has a higher mean.
Optional: The new result updating the surrogate.

prompts.prompt: How does successive halving decide which trials get more training?
sketch: Core: Trials ranked on a small budget, the top share kept with a larger cumulative budget and the rest stopped, repeated until one remains; the cumulative limit is distinguished from the extra training in each round.
Optional: The total budget used.
